questions.stem: Why does the study design ask students to read and re-read mentor texts?
options: to prepare a formal analytical essay on each of the three mentor texts
to discover the single correct way in which an idea should be written about
to learn the mechanics of effective writing and apply them in their own
to memorise long passages that can be reproduced word for word in the exam
questions.explanation: Mentor texts are models of effective and cohesive writing, read closely so students can borrow and adapt their techniques. Reproducing them word for word would not be the student's own writing.

questions.stem: In the study of writing, adapting a mentor text means:
options: reshaping its ideas, form or structure into a new text of your own
copying the mentor text closely, changing only the characters' names
writing a summary of the mentor text's main ideas in your own words
analysing the mentor text's language in a formal analytical essay
questions.explanation: The study design describes students experimenting with adaptation, taking something from a mentor text and transforming it. Changing only the names is copying, not adaptation.

questions.stem: Mentor text A builds suspense through very short paragraphs; mentor text B builds it through long, winding sentences. The most useful conclusion a student can draw is that:
options: short paragraphs are the only reliable way that any writer can build suspense
suspense is a technique that belongs in fiction and cannot work in non-fiction
different techniques can achieve similar effects, so she should choose what suits her piece
one of the two mentor texts must be poorly written, since the techniques are opposites
questions.explanation: Comparing mentor texts shows that effects come from how a technique is handled in context, not from one fixed rule. Opposite techniques can both succeed, so neither text is shown to be weak.

questions.stem: In the study design, a 'specific and situated audience' is one that is:
options: a group of readers who already share exactly the same views as the writer does
clearly defined and located in a particular context where the text is received
anyone, anywhere, who might ever happen to come across the text in future
the teacher who marks the piece, since no one else will ever read it
questions.explanation: A situated audience has a defined identity and a context, such as parents reading a school newsletter. Writing for 'anyone, anywhere' is the opposite of a situated audience.

questions.stem: A student arguing that her school should keep its library revises 'Libraries are sort of important' to 'Libraries are essential.' The revision serves her purpose better mainly because:
options: the revision shifts her purpose from arguing to reflecting
the revision makes the sentence more colloquial in its register
removing the hedge makes her stance confident and clear
the revised sentence now supplies evidence for the claim it makes
questions.explanation: Writing to argue calls for a firm position, and 'sort of' weakens it. The revision adds no evidence; it simply sharpens the claim.

questions.stem: In a reflective piece, a writer deliberately writes: 'Perhaps I was afraid, or perhaps I was only tired.' The tentative language suits the purpose mainly because it:
options: signals to readers that the piece is fiction rather than memoir
conveys honest uncertainty as the writer works through an experience
states a firm position that the reader is being urged to adopt
explains the physical and scientific causes of the writer's tiredness that day
questions.explanation: Reflection explores experiences of personal discovery, and 'perhaps' shows the writer still weighing what happened. A firm position to adopt would suit writing to argue.

questions.stem: A student's piece recounts her family's farm being sold, then closes by urging readers to buy from local growers. Using the study design's purposes, the piece moves:
options: from arguing to expressing
from expressing to arguing
from explaining to reflecting
from reflecting to explaining
questions.explanation: A recount of events is expressive writing, and urging readers to act is arguing. The piece ends, rather than begins, with the argument.

questions.stem: A student writes a speech for a memorial service for a teacher, to an audience of grieving staff, parents and students. Which choice best suits this context?
options: a formal report listing the teacher's employment history year by year
an argument about how the school's leadership ought to be run in future
a measured, sincere tone with specific memories that many listeners share
a comic routine built on in-jokes that only his closest friends will recognise
questions.explanation: A mixed, grieving audience needs sincerity and memories they can share. In-jokes exclude most listeners, and a report or argument ignores the purpose of the occasion.

questions.stem: Writing an open letter to her younger self, a student uses nicknames and private jokes. This choice is effective mainly because:
options: private jokes make any piece of writing more cohesive for all readers
the close social connection between writer and addressee suits a familiar register
open letters must always use slang if they are to be published successfully in print
the piece is aimed at a formal audience that the writer has never met
questions.explanation: The study design asks how well writer and audience know each other, and no one knows the writer better than her younger self. The addressee is intimate, not unknown.

questions.stem: A student writes for her school's online newsletter, which is read mainly by parents. She opens in heavy teenage slang to sound relatable. What is the main risk of this choice?
options: slang is not permitted in any piece of writing that is published online
the piece will become far too formal and distant for its parent readers
the slang will make her argument more convincing to most of the parents
the register may alienate the adult audience and weaken her credibility
questions.explanation: Register should match the situated audience, and slang aimed at teenagers may put off parents. Slang makes writing less formal, not more.

questions.stem: A student writing to explain traces how a local mine's closure led to shops shutting, then to families leaving the town. Which structure best suits this purpose?
options: a cause-and-effect sequence linked by connectives such as 'as a result'
a series of disconnected images, presented with no links between them
a debate transcript in which two opposing speakers trade arguments
a poem with a strict rhyme scheme and a repeated refrain in each stanza
questions.explanation: Explaining explores cause and effect, so a linked sequence of consequences fits the purpose. Disconnected images would hide the chain of causes the student wants to show.

questions.stem: A student writing to explain why young people are leaving her town wants to stay credible. Which sentence best suits her purpose?
options: Oh, how my heart weeps for the empty streets and shopfronts of my childhood!
Leave now, before this town swallows your future the way it swallowed mine!
With the last bus leaving at six, jobs in the city are hard for teenagers here to reach.
Everyone knows this town is a dump, and nobody with any sense would choose to stay.
questions.explanation: A specific, verifiable cause supports an explanation and keeps the writer credible. The insult is a sweeping claim, and the exclamations suit expressing or arguing rather than explaining.

questions.stem: A student is writing about a bushfire evacuation and wants readers to feel the confusion of the moment. Which point of view best serves this aim?
options: close first person, limited to what one fleeing character can see and hear
omniscient narration that explains every family's plan before the fire arrives
a detached report of the fire's statistics, written after the event is over
a narrator who is told the outcome of the fire before the story begins
questions.explanation: Limiting the view to one frightened person withholds the big picture, so readers share the confusion. Knowing every plan or the outcome in advance removes it.

questions.stem: A student turns a spoken monologue into a printed short story. Which change best suits the print mode?
options: replacing vocal emphasis with punctuation, italics and paragraphing
adding stage directions describing the speaker's tone of voice for readers
repeating key lines often so that listeners do not lose track of the story
removing all description, since readers can already picture the speaker
questions.explanation: In print, readers cannot hear tone or emphasis, so the page must carry it through punctuation and layout. Frequent repetition helps listeners, not readers, who can look back.

questions.stem: A personal piece is built from six short, separately titled vignettes, each set in a different year. This structure mainly:
options: means the sections need no shared links, images or patterns at all
turns the piece into an argument that ends with a call to action
shows change across time through fragments the reader connects
presents one continuous scene that unfolds over a single afternoon
questions.explanation: Vignettes from different years let readers piece together change across a life. They still rely on links and patterns, or the piece would not cohere.

questions.stem: A student writes a story about a breakup entirely as a series of unsent text messages. This form is most effective at:
options: turning the piece into a formal argument about the effects of technology
keeping the story within the conventions of Standard Australian English
creating intimacy and gaps that invite readers to infer what went unsaid
giving an objective, omniscient account of both partners' private thoughts
questions.explanation: Messages never sent are private and fragmentary, so readers fill in the silences. They come from only one partner, so the account is neither objective nor omniscient.

questions.stem: A reflective piece describes learning a new language as 'a house I'm building room by room', returning to doors, windows and foundations throughout. This is:
options: a flashback that reveals the writer's early childhood
an example of onomatopoeia imitating building sounds
an extended metaphor that structures the reflection
a single simile, used once for decorative effect only
questions.explanation: The comparison is developed across the whole piece, which makes it an extended metaphor. It returns repeatedly and uses no 'like' or 'as', so it is not a one-off simile.

questions.stem: ‘We marched for the river. We marched for the trees. We marched because no one else would.’ The repeated opening is an example of:
options: anaphora, building rhythm and a sense of resolve
an oxymoron, joining two contradictory words together
a rhetorical question, implying an answer the reader shares
enjambment, running a sentence over the end of a line
questions.explanation: Anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive sentences, here 'We marched'. The sentences are statements, so there is no rhetorical question.

questions.stem: Which revision best strengthens the cohesion between two paragraphs of an explanatory piece?
options: ending the first paragraph with an exclamation mark to keep the reader alert
beginning the second with 'This loss of habitat, in turn,' to link cause and effect
beginning the second paragraph with an anecdote on a completely new subject
replacing the second paragraph's first sentence with a quotation from an expert
questions.explanation: The phrase refers back to the previous paragraph and signals a consequence, tying the two together. An anecdote on a new subject would break the connection rather than build it.

questions.stem: A story's narration is playful for most of its length, then turns stark in the final paragraph as the narrator's dog dies. This shift in tone is effective mainly because:
options: the contrast heightens the impact of the loss
a consistent tone is never valued in effective writing
it switches the point of view into the second person
it reveals that the story's events were only a dream
questions.explanation: After so much lightness, the sudden starkness makes the death land harder. A consistent tone is often valuable; this shift works because of its placement.

questions.stem: A student revises 'Poverty is hard' to 'In winter, Mum ran the heater for an hour, then switched it off and handed us blankets.' The revision is stronger mainly because:
options: a concrete, specific image makes the abstract idea felt
it adds a statistic that supports the claim about poverty
it shifts the whole text into a more formal register
it uses technical vocabulary to explain how poverty works
questions.explanation: A specific detail lets readers experience hardship rather than be told about it. The revision contains no statistic or technical terms.

questions.stem: ‘The jetty's pylons stood in the low tide like the ribs of something drowned.’ The simile mainly:
options: uses personification to make the jetty speak aloud
creates humour through deliberate exaggeration
creates an eerie image that hints at loss
presents neutral detail about how the jetty was built
questions.explanation: Comparing pylons to the ribs of a drowned creature gives the scene a haunting, mournful quality. The comparison uses 'like', so it is a simile, not personification.

questions.stem: A memoir about a car accident is written in the present tense: 'The glass is everywhere. I can't find my phone.' The main effect is:
options: distance, signalling calm reflection on the crash years afterwards
objectivity, presenting the events as a neutral police record
uncertainty about whether the accident really happened at all
immediacy, placing the reader inside the moment as it unfolds
questions.explanation: Present tense makes events feel as if they are happening now, drawing the reader into the confusion. Calm, distant reflection is more often signalled by the past tense.

questions.stem: ‘I waited — for the call, for the knock, for anything.’ The dash in this sentence mainly:
options: shows that a word has been left out of a quotation
signals that a different character is now speaking
creates a pause that sets up a building list
marks the beginning of a line of direct speech
questions.explanation: The dash holds the reader for a beat before the list of what she waited for, which builds to 'anything'. There is no speech or quotation in the sentence.

questions.stem: Which opening line most effectively hooks the reader of a short story?
options: ‘This is a story about my grandmother and a car that she once drove.’
‘It was a normal day, just like any other day had been before it.’
‘Hello, my name is Jess, and I am going to tell you all a story.’
‘The night Gran stole the ute, she was eighty-three and wearing her slippers.’
questions.explanation: The line raises immediate questions and builds character through surprising, specific detail. The others announce or flatten the story instead of drawing readers in.

questions.stem: A dramatic monologue is:
options: a conversation between two characters of equal status and power in a scene
a narrator's summary of events, told from outside the story
a list of stage directions for actors performing in a play
a speech by one character to a silent listener, revealing who they are
questions.explanation: In a dramatic monologue one character speaks and, often without meaning to, reveals their personality. A conversation between characters is dialogue.

questions.stem: A student writes an argument in the voice of a frustrated bus driver, though she has never driven a bus herself. This choice:
options: uses a persona to give the argument an authentic, situated voice
breaks the rule that writers may only ever write in their own voice and identity
turns the piece into a reflective memoir of her own experiences
removes any need for the writer to consider her audience
questions.explanation: Writers often adopt personas, and the study design encourages students to explore voices that suit purpose and context. There is no rule restricting writers to their own identity.

questions.stem: A student writing a monologue for a 70-year-old fisherman has him say words like 'leveraging' and 'synergy'. Why does this undermine the piece?
options: the words are too short and plain to sound authentic in a monologue
the monologue is written in the first person rather than the third
the corporate jargon clashes with the voice the character's context suggests
monologues must never contain any technical or specialised vocabulary at all
questions.explanation: Voice should fit the character, purpose and context, and boardroom jargon jars with a fisherman's world unless it is a deliberate joke. Technical vocabulary is fine when it suits the speaker, so it is not banned.

questions.stem: A writer uses sentence fragments such as 'Dust. Heat. Nothing.' in a story. This is best described as:
options: an error that always weakens creative writing and must be fixed
a list of technical terms written for an expert audience
a convention that is required in formal written reports
a deliberate non-standard choice for emphasis and atmosphere
questions.explanation: The study design allows non-standard conventions where they suit the purpose, and fragments can create stark atmosphere. They would be out of place in a formal report.

questions.stem: In a memoir, a writer leaves her grandmother's words in Vietnamese, untranslated, beside the English narration. The most likely intended effect is to:
options: follow a convention requiring every memoir to be written in two languages
convey the grandmother's voice and the gap between languages the writer lives with
exclude every English-speaking reader from understanding any part of the memoir
show readers that the writer has forgotten how to speak Vietnamese herself
questions.explanation: Keeping the words untranslated preserves the grandmother's voice and lets readers feel the space between languages. The English narration remains, so readers are not shut out of the memoir.

questions.stem: In a formal opinion piece, which sentence follows the conventions of Standard Australian English?
options: Less students are walking to school, which affects there health.
Fewer students are walking to school, which affects their health.
Less students are walking to school, which effects their health.
Fewer students are walking to school, which effects their health.
questions.explanation: Formal writing uses 'fewer' for things that are counted, and 'affects' is the verb needed here. 'Effects' as a verb means 'brings about', and 'there' should be 'their'.

questions.stem: To enrich a piece about personal journeys, a student keeps a notebook of overheard phrases and small observations on her daily train trip. This mainly:
options: replaces the need for her to draft and then revise her finished piece
ensures that her piece will follow one of the mentor texts exactly
proves that her finished piece is factual rather than imaginative
gathers authentic detail and voices she can draw on when drafting
questions.explanation: The study design encourages students to observe and record their own experiences to enrich their writing. Gathering ideas comes before drafting; it does not replace it.

questions.stem: After drafting, a student reads her story aloud and notices she has used 'suddenly' five times. Cutting most of them is part of:
options: pre-writing, choosing the idea and form
refining, sharpening the language for effect
brainstorming, gathering the first ideas
publishing, presenting the final copy
questions.explanation: Refining polishes a draft's language, for example by removing repetition. Brainstorming and pre-writing happen before any draft exists.

questions.stem: Why might a writer read a draft aloud before finalising it?
options: to confirm that the font, spacing and layout are consistent on every page
to hear rhythm, clumsy phrasing and repetition that silent reading can miss
to check that the word count of the draft falls within the set word limit
to find the spelling errors that a computer's spellchecker has already underlined
questions.explanation: Hearing the words exposes awkward rhythm and repetition the eye skims over. Word counts, spellchecks and layout are checked by looking, not listening.

questions.stem: A teacher comments that a student's opinion piece 'preaches to the converted'. The best revision is to:
options: rewrite the piece as a narrative that contains no argument
anticipate a sceptical reader's objections and address them
add more praise for readers who already agree with her view
remove the contention so that readers can decide for themselves
questions.explanation: Preaching to the converted means writing only for readers who already agree, so the fix is to engage those who do not. Removing the contention would abandon the purpose of arguing.

questions.stem: In a writing workshop, which piece of peer feedback is most useful?
options: ‘It's good. I really liked it a lot, and I don't think you need to change anything.’
‘You should probably just write about something else entirely next time.’
‘Change your story so that it is more like the one I wrote for this task.’
‘In scene two the dialogue tells us what Sam feels; could his actions show it instead?’
questions.explanation: Useful feedback is specific and suggests a direction the writer can test. Vague praise gives the writer nothing to act on.

questions.stem: A commentary reflecting on writing processes should mainly:
options: explain the choices made in the written text and their intended effects
summarise the plot or content of the written text in the order it unfolds
give the written text a rating out of ten and justify the score awarded
list every mentor text that the student has read during the whole year
questions.explanation: The study design asks students to explain the decisions they made through their writing processes. A summary of content explains no decisions.

questions.stem: Which commentary sentence best links a writing choice to the intended audience?
options: Because my readers are Year 7s new to the school, I kept sentences short and used 'you' to reassure them.
I chose to write about starting secondary school because I thought it was an interesting topic.
My piece is 850 words long and is divided into four parts, each with its own heading.
I used many language features in my piece, such as similes, metaphors and alliteration.
questions.explanation: The sentence names a specific audience, the choices made for it, and the intended effect. Listing techniques without purpose or effect is a common weakness in commentaries.

questions.stem: Which commentary sentence best explains how a mentor text influenced the student's writing?
options: My text copies the mentor text's opening paragraph closely so that its influence is easy to see.
The mentor text was written by an author who has won a major prize for her essays.
Like the mentor essay's use of one object to frame memory, I used my grandfather's watch to anchor each section.
I read the mentor text three times and found that it was very well written and quite enjoyable.
questions.explanation: The sentence identifies a specific technique in the mentor text and shows how it was adapted. Copying an opening is not influence but reproduction.

questions.stem: Which commentary sentence best reflects on the implications of a writing choice?
options: The ending of my piece takes place at the beach, just after the two sisters' fight.
I wrote the ending last of all because it was the hardest part of the piece to write.
Leaving the argument unresolved risks frustrating some readers, but it suits my piece's uncertainty.
My ending is perfect, and I am confident that every reader will find it satisfying.
questions.explanation: Reflecting on implications means weighing a choice's effect on readers, including its risks. Describing where the ending is set explains no choice at all.
